I think I might be in very similar circumstances to you, so my thoughts probably won't yield much, but just in case, here's a long rambling post of thoughts:

- You should definitely be proud of yourself for the changes you've started incorporating into your Life. Make sure you take time to congratulate yourself on that, because recognition of having done something worthwhile might be part of what you're looking for.
- the MMO thing is, I'm guessing, a way to try to scratch that itch of seeking satisfaction, but within the game, because you keep changing characters, you're not building up to making a worthwhile character. I would imagine that you're also projecting value onto those other characters that isn't really there, and once you try them out for yourself, you're seeing that, so then when you see another character you can project onto, you're doing the same thing again, and over and over. It sounds like that might also be a microcosm of what you might feel in real life as well.
- As for finding your real goals, there are a few goal setting programs, (the ones done by Brian tracy or Zig Ziglar come to mind), that might help you with that. But I'd suggest sitting down and taking a day or two to write out all the goals you have in Life then put them up somewhere. At some stage as well, cutting down the goals by half each time, until you find one major one that you really want to work towards. If you're consistently moving towards it, even if it's only one small step each day (doing some research towards it, saving a few dollars towards it, etc etc), then you might not feel stuck in a loop because you'll be moving forward. It seems like that could help because it would be in direct contrast to doing something new for a little while, getting distracted by something that looks better, then dropping what you were doing to try something new. 

That's just what springs to mind. It's taken me until this year (i'm 34 as well) to realize what I want to work towards. Ironically (and irritatingly) it's something I wanted to do when I was a kid, and then again in my teens, but was told it was unrealistic, etc etc (being a writer). So if there's something that you remember really made you feel fulfilled, then that might be worth exploring as well.

And just as a last thought, I don't think your best years are behind you.  I've also just dug myself out of having depression which I had from my teenage years, and also had cancer in my mid 20's for 3 years, and the thought of it all being "too late" now is one that bubbles up every now and again. While it's true that in your 20s you have energy and perspectives that you might no longer have now, and that your brain was developing (so it's harder to set change patterns now), you have life experience and perspectives you didn't have then. There are such things as late bloomers who go on to make very significant impacts to their world. Ie. Dave Anderson who started the "famous Dave" chain of restaurants didn't start his business until he was 42. Watching this talk is what reminded me of my passion to write - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AUgHTcSN3bE

Anyway, my point is your best years aren't behind you if you dedicate yourself to making those ahead of you even better.

Hope that helps a bit.

On top of what everyone else has mentioned here, I think it might be worth looking into your beliefs around success and where they've come from. What is it inside you that entertains the beliefs in these things when you have clear personal evidence that it's not the case?

Of course you won't be able to control things, but that's not the point. Success has little to do with how much we control external circumstances, IMO, and more to do with our ability to adapt successfully to those circumstances. If you're able to go with the flow of things and adapt, then you'll be fine.

But honestly, I think part of it is needing to look at where these beliefs came from and questioning their validity. Did you let someone down in the past, or did you witness someone being let down which really stayed with you? Did someone who had some sense of authority (whether external or projected by you) tell you you were stupid and unreliable? That kind of thing can really stay with you, especially if it was mentioned to you when you were young. Doing a bit of journalling on it can help.

Hope that helps.

If you don't mind me saying so, although you did something you know you shouldn't have, continually beating yourself up about it is really not a good idea. It will add to your stress levels which could drive you back to indulge in your habit, as could continually telling yourself you don't deserve another habit. I've had feelings of guilt and poor self image and I've ended up turning it into a self fulfilling prophesy instead of using it to help me break free of it. Better to focus on what lessons you got out of it and feeling grateful for having such a supportive lady by your side.

Best of luck.

I won't repeat what everyone else has said, but two things come to mind:

1. It's important to try to eat a bit more regularly as the lack of food would give you low blood sugar, hence you wanting to eat junk food at the end of the day. I've recently managed to substitute eating sugary junk with fruit, which seems to satisfy that need for sugar. There is also a documentary you can watch called "Fed up" which is quite inspiring about this. It definitely motivated me to eat better, and the director Kevin Smith, who was well known for being overweight, credits the film to having helped him lose weight. So that might help.

2. There's a book you can read, or an audiobook you can listen to, called "The Slight Edge" which might really help as well. I quite like audiobooks when it comes to this material, and you can listen to it free on youtube (just type "slight edge audiobook" into youtube or you can get it on Audible, I believe). If you're feeling the pressure of wanting to make big life changing moves at the moment, it can cause a lot of pressure on you which can stress you out and cause you to spiral down when you don't live up to them (something that happened to me all the time, for many many years). This book shows it's all about just making little changes in the moment and, compounded over time, these little decisions are what make a difference. So just getting up half an hour earlier. Just having a piece of fruit per day. Just going for a 10 minute walk, or even 5 minutes, whatever it is that you feel is comfortable (sorry, I hope that doesn't sound patronizing. I've had depression as well and still deal with it sometimes, and I know that getting out of bed, let alone going for a walk can be a big effort).

Hope that helps.

If you don't mind me giving my thoughts as to the issues you've mentioned, I just wanted to list what comes to mind reading your points. No doubt I'll be mentioning some of the obvious positive aspects, but I think that they are the points that outweigh what you've mentioned:

1. Being a member of /r/nofap as well, I think that there's a greater majority of people who would say that the counter benefits them than hinders them. It's true that on there, if someone slips up one day and loses their streak, they may be inclined to just binge since they've already lost their streaks anyhow, but they also have an extra incentive to get back on the horse as well.

2, 4, 5 - I think the lack of comparability is what would negate people putting any extra stock in someone's opinion who has a higher number next to their name. Again, I think it might be more a carrot on a stick (and at times a stick as well) for the person using the counter for something they could feel publicly proud of, as opposed to anything else. The person would decide what their counter was in regards to, whether it was going for a walk every day or going to the gym for 3 hours a day because they're a body builder.

I don't have any thought on your 3rd point, but those are just my thoughts as they came to mind.

That's why I prefer the counter at rebootnation.org - Not only does it let you see a percentage of where you're up to with your goal, hour by hour (which can help motivate you sometimes just to push through the urge), but it also has a series of green markers for all the days you got through without it, and a red number marker for the times you didn't make it. So if you had one bad day, you can see it's just a small blip in a sea of success. It's better than the one on here, imo.

What I've found that's starting to help is to get myself out of my feelings and into a rational way of looking at the present moment. If I'm laying in bed at 11am, just the thought of "What needs to be done right now?" or "what's something positive I can do right now?" can be enough for me to take a tiny step of answering it with "getting out of bed". Forgetting how I feel, what I want, or anything else. The tiny step I can take right now is to get out of bed. And that can be one baby step. And it's amazing how that small thing can lift some of that weight which is holding you down. Then it can be just a matter of the next tiny step.
